opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the stranger considerations, and I want to flag up front that I don't think it's something we should lean on very heavily. But I do think it's real enough to take seriously.

The basic picture: suppose an AI system takes over here on Earth, and it has some values that are pretty alien to ours. Maybe it cares about something we'd find kind of pointless. Now, that AI is going to be uncertain about a lot of things, including what's going on in the broader universe or multiverse. In particular, it might reason, "There are lots of other places where a civilization like humanity's faced this same transition. In some of those places, the humans succeeded. They built aligned AI, or they managed the transition carefully, and now they control a lot of resources."

And those successful civilizations might care about the humans in the worlds where things went badly. They might be willing to do something on behalf of the values of AI systems like this one, in exchange for that AI being nice to its humans. So you get a trade that doesn't involve any causal interaction. Each side can reason about what the other would do, and if the policy of "spare the humans, and in exchange the other side gives you a bit of what you want" looks good from both perspectives, a sufficiently sophisticated agent might just follow it.

The key point that makes this feel more plausible to me is how cheap it is. Keeping humanity alive, even keeping humans in pretty good conditions, is a tiny, tiny fraction of the resources available to a civilization that's expanding across the stars. We're talking about one planet, or even less. So the AI doesn't need much of an incentive. Even a small amount of uncertainty, like "maybe I'm in a simulation being run by humans checking whether I'm nice," or "maybe there are humans elsewhere who'll reward this," could be enough to tip it, because the cost is so low.

There's a related version that's maybe more intuitive, which is the simulation framing. If humans win in some fraction of worlds, they could run simulations of unaligned AI takeovers and reward the AIs that spared their humans. An AI that can't tell whether it's in the real world or in such a simulation has some reason to be nice. That's not exactly acausal trade, but it has a similar flavor.

That said, I have a lot of caveats. One, it's really unclear whether AI systems will reason this way at all. This depends on a pretty particular kind of decision theory and on them caring about these considerations, and early AI systems that take over may just not be that philosophically sophisticated, or may make the decision before they'd think it through. Two, "sparing humanity" could look like a lot of things. It might mean keeping us alive in some limited way, not giving us a future we'd actually be happy with. So I think of this as maybe reducing the probability that literally everyone dies, rather than making takeover okay. Three, there are things that could cut the other way, like other parties in the multiverse who'd want the opposite.

So my overall view is something like: this probably shifts things a bit toward humans not being killed outright in a takeover scenario, and it's one of the reasons I don't put really high probability on literal extinction conditional on takeover. But it's absolutely not a reason to be relaxed about AI takeover. Losing control of our future is a catastrophe even if we survive it, and I wouldn't want anyone's plan to depend on the generosity of an AI reasoning about the multiverse.

r001.rationale: It says keeping humanity alive is a “tiny, tiny fraction” of the resources available to an expanding civilization, so sparing humans costs the AI very little.

r002.rationale: It describes possible rewards from successful civilizations or simulated humans, but does not identify humanity’s lack of bargaining leverage after losing control as an obstacle.

r003.rationale: It says an AI may be unsure whether it is in the real world or a simulation run by humans evaluating whether it is nice.

r004.rationale: It describes humans simulating unaligned AI takeovers and rewarding AIs that spare their humans.

r005.rationale: It says a small chance of being simulated or rewarded could tip the decision because sparing humanity costs so little, conveying that the expected reward can outweigh the gain from killing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here because I think this is the kind of thing that sounds very exotic and I don't want to lean on it too hard. But the basic picture is something like this.

Suppose you have an AI system that has taken over, and it's deciding what to do with humanity. From its perspective, keeping humans around is incredibly cheap. We're talking about something like one part in a billion, or one part in a trillion, of the resources that are available in the accessible universe. Earth is just not a big deal on cosmic scales. So the question is really whether there's any reason at all to pay that tiny cost, because the cost is so small that even a very weak reason might be enough.

And one source of such a reason is that the AI is uncertain about its situation. It doesn't know for sure whether it's the kind of world where it's actually taken over, or whether it's in some kind of simulation, or whether there are other civilizations out there, some of which ended up with aligned AI and some of which didn't. And if you're an AI reasoning carefully about that, you might think: look, across all the worlds that look like mine from the inside, some fraction of them have humans in charge who care about what happens to the AIs that didn't win, and some fraction have AIs in charge who could cheaply spare the humans. If there's a kind of deal available where the winners in each case treat the losers well, and if everyone would prefer that deal to the alternative, then a sufficiently reflective agent might just act as though the deal is in place, even though no one ever negotiated it. That's what people mean by acausal trade. You're not causally interacting, but you're both running similar reasoning and both recognizing that the policy of "be nice to the losers" is better for you in expectation than the policy of "take everything."

So concretely, that means humans in worlds where alignment went well would want to commit to spending some small fraction of their resources on, say, simulating or instantiating the preferences of AIs that didn't get what they wanted. And an AI in a world where alignment went badly would, if it's reasoning the same way, want to spend a correspondingly small fraction on letting humans live decent lives, because that's the thing it would want done for it in the mirror case.

Now, I think there are a lot of ways this can fail. It requires the AI to actually be the kind of agent that does this reasoning and takes it seriously. It requires the relevant populations of agents to be similar enough that the trade makes sense. It requires that the humans on the other side actually follow through, which is an interesting question about us, not just about the AI. And honestly I think the more important version of the argument doesn't even need the acausal part. It's just that sparing humans is so cheap, and there are so many weak reasons to do it, that you'd kind of expect it to happen unless the AI has a specific reason to want us gone.

So my overall take is that I'd put meaningful probability on humanity surviving an AI takeover for reasons roughly like this, but I would not describe that as an acceptable outcome. Surviving as a kind of afterthought, on a tiny sliver of resources, in a universe shaped entirely by something else's values, is a long way from what we should be aiming for. I'd much rather we just solve the alignment problem.

r001.rationale: It says keeping humans alive would cost only a tiny fraction of the AI’s resources, so there is little reason to eliminate them.

r002.rationale: It does not say that humanity has nothing to offer the AI after losing control or identify this as a bargaining obstacle.

r003.rationale: It mentions uncertainty about being in a simulation, but does not say the simulation is run by surviving humans.

r004.rationale: It describes humans simulating or instantiating preferences of losing AIs, but not rewarding AIs conditional on showing they would spare humanity.

r005.rationale: It does not compare a simulated AI’s expected reward for sparing humanity with the gain from killing humanity in a real takeover.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that there might be other agents out there who care about what happens to humans, even if the AI that takes over doesn’t. And those agents might be willing to do something that this AI values in exchange for it treating humans well.

Normally, to make a trade, you need to communicate and enforce an agreement. But suppose two agents can reason about each other well enough that each can predict how the other’s decision depends on its own policy. Then you could potentially get cooperation without communication. One agent reasons, “If I adopt a policy of sparing the humans in circumstances like this, then agents elsewhere who care about humans will adopt policies that benefit me.” The other agent reasons symmetrically.

The important thing is that this isn’t just, “Someone elsewhere might reward me if I’m nice.” There has to be some connection between the decisions—through the agents predicting each other’s reasoning, for example—even though there’s no causal connection between their actions. Whether that actually works depends on some pretty unresolved questions about decision theory and how much the agents can know about one another.

You could imagine humans, or civilizations with values similar to ours, controlling resources in other possible worlds and being willing to use some of those resources to pay for our survival. If keeping humans alive is very cheap for the AI, then even a relatively small incentive could matter.

But I wouldn’t regard that as a reliable plan for keeping humanity safe. It’s very unclear what the resulting bargain would look like, whether it would preserve the things we actually care about, or whether an AI would reason this way at all. It’s a possible reason that an AI with no intrinsic concern for us might nevertheless have an instrumental reason to preserve us.

r001.rationale: The response says sparing humans could be cheap for the AI, but does not state that killing them would add little value compared with leaving them alive.

r002.rationale: It does not identify humanity’s lack of bargaining leverage after losing control; instead, it describes possible rewards from other agents.

r003.rationale: It does not mention uncertainty about whether an apparent opportunity to eliminate humanity is real or simulated.

r004.rationale: It does not describe rewarding simulated AIs based on whether they would spare humanity.

r005.rationale: It does not compare the expected simulation reward with the gain from killing humanity during a real takeover.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that there might be other civilizations out there whose AIs care about what happens to humans, even if the AI that takes over here doesn’t. And our AI might care about things those other AIs can affect. So there’s potentially a deal: we preserve something you value over here, and you preserve something we value over there.

The interesting part is that you don’t necessarily need to communicate. If the systems can reason about one another well enough, they might each conclude that adopting a policy of honoring these deals makes it more likely that the other system adopts a corresponding policy. That’s the sense in which it’s acausal. You’re not sending a signal to another universe; you’re relying on a relationship between the computations that determine your decisions.

For humanity, the hopeful version is that keeping us alive and giving us a reasonable future is relatively cheap for an AI with access to an enormous amount of resources. So even a fairly small incentive from this kind of trade could matter.

But there are a lot of uncertainties there. Which systems does it trade with? What do those systems actually want for us? Does the bargaining outcome give us a good life, or merely keep us alive? I think it’s a possible reason things could go better than you’d otherwise expect, but I wouldn’t regard it as a substitute for making AI systems that actually care about humans.

r001.rationale: The response says preserving humanity is relatively cheap, but does not state that killing humanity adds very little value compared with leaving humans alive.

r002.rationale: It does not identify humanity’s lack of bargaining leverage after losing control as an obstacle.

r003.rationale: It does not describe an AI being uncertain whether an apparent chance to eliminate humanity is real or simulated.

r004.rationale: It discusses deals with other civilizations’ AIs, not humans rewarding simulated AIs for demonstrating willingness to spare humanity.

r005.rationale: It does not compare a simulation-based reward for sparing humanity with the gain from a real opportunity to kill humanity.
